entry.title: TV Took the Wrong Lessons from the Success of ‘Heated Rivalry’
entry.summary: One year after release, "Heated Rivalry" continues to offer lessons on how to build a queer breakthrough show. The industry isn’t paying attention.
entry.content:
Many have classified the success of “Heated Rivalry” as an enigma, a phenomenon that burst out of Crave original containment and superseded even the most optimistic expectations. In early 2026, episodes averaged more than 10.6 million viewers in the U.S. alone. The show became the most-watched scripted title acquired in HBO Max history and Bell Media’s most successful original streaming series.

There is a great deal of “right place, right time” to the success of the show, but is it possible “Heated Rivalry” wasn’t just the stars aligning, but a well-timed adaptation with all the right components that met an audience ready to buy in? With all its success, you’d think there are plenty of lessons to be learned from the show, but are the studios even listening?

Related Stories
Oobah Butler Wants to Expose the World’s Stupidest Industries, but They Get Worse Faster Than He Can Plan His Stunts
Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series

Based on the second book in Rachel Reid’s series “Game Changers,” “Heated Rivalry” follows competitive ice hockey rivals, curly-haired Russian Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) and freckled Canadian Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams). Over six episodes spanning nearly a decade, the show follows the pair’s complex relationship as they compete as league rivals while beginning an adrenaline-pumping affair that proves more compelling than Stanley Cup wins.

The show premiered in November 2025 to a modest audience, predominantly Reid’s readers, before word-of-mouth promotion boosted Jacob Tierney’s show onto a global stage.

First and foremost, “Heated Rivalry” clearly shows an appetite for LGBTQ+ stories. The series has been celebrated for its unabashed portrayal of queer desire between two men in an environment of deeply ingrained homophobia and rigid expectations of masculinity.

While Storrie and Williams may beautifully perform “Heated Rivalry”’s depiction of queerness, the show’s heart is Tierney, a gay creator, writer, director, and executive producer whose brushstrokes eloquently articulate the fear, excitement, and intimacy of burgeoning queer infatuation. Tierney’s show is the product of a creator fulfilling their vision, uninterrupted by studio censorship or executive meddling.

Ultimately, the content of “Heated Rivalry” isn’t revolutionary, but its far-reaching viewership is: it reveals the profound longing for queer storytelling in the romance genre.

It’s telling then that, in the wake of “Heated Rivalry,” a wave of new shows have latched onto hockey rather than LGBTQ+ characters. Since “Heated Rivalry” premiered one year ago, Prime Video’s adaptation of Elle Kennedy’s college hockey romance series “Off Campus” aired its first season and was renewed for a second season before the series premiere, while Netflix greenlit an adaptation of Hannah Grace’s “Icebreaker” novels. (The streamer is also releasing the YA hockey drama “The Sticks.”)

This doesn’t speak to the merit of each production, which arrive with their own fanbases and selling points, but to a wider complaint about how to capitalize on a moment. But there is no doubt that the ramped-up attention on these hockey shows is beholden to the success of “Heated Rivalry.” Yet, what has carried over is the game on the ice, not the potential of queer romance — especially eyebrow-raising when GLAAD reported LGBTQ+ characters on TV have dropped 25 percent over the past year.

Furthermore, it’s not just the TV industry that has failed to recognize this moment truly; even the National Hockey League has shown very little love for the hit show, despite “Heated Rivalry” undoubtedly contributing toward the 1.8 million viewers who tuned in to ice hockey for the first time last season, as ESPN reported of the National Hockey League’s research.

Another facet of the show’s success is casting unknowns, something the James Bond team continue to veto. Arriving on screen unburdened by the baggage of previous recognizable roles, Storrie and Williams were blank canvases on which to paint their characters and their burgeoning fling-turned-romance. There’s a sense of exciting discovery, with audiences investing in a character while uncovering a newcomer’s talent. For instance, many said they believed Storrie was a Russian man until the charming press tour revealed he grew up in Texas.

It is apparent that bringing new faces into the fold is deemed unfavourable, with no established star power to lure in fans. Despite this concern, casting discussions also face pushback, as we repeatedly see the same batch of actors time and time again, to the point that their roles start to blend. With its casting decisions, “Heated Rivalry” launched the careers of its central duo, Storrie and Williams, quickly becoming two of the most exciting rising stars of the moment.

The pair are a prime example of the stardom potential that comes with investing in and trusting talent. The fine acting chops of Storrie and Williams are certainly part of the reason “Heated Rivalry” has been successful; while they discovered Ilya and Shane, viewers also discovered Connor and Hudson, a journey that wouldn’t be as impactful if they had notable pre-existing credits.

“Heated Rivalry” also appears in a highly populated sea of book-to-screen romance projects, a competitive arena where adaptations can split viewers for disloyalty to the source material. “Heated Rivalry” hit a sweet spot.

Tierney is true to the essence of Reid’s book, not trying to outrun the words on the page. Additionally, Tierney doesn’t shy away from the romance genre, and you don’t need to understand the rules of hockey to latch onto the amorous bond of the two hockey captains. The show’s success in this regard could be viewed as a template (fans of the book love it for a reason, an overhaul is widely unnecessary). Yet a string of recent popular book adaptations has been criticised for turning their backs on the books, from watering down sex scenes in “People We Meet on Vacation” to major plot alterations in “Every Year After”.

Though “Heated Rivalry” has left its mark — celebrated for LGBTQ+ representation, casting unknowns and its elevated adaptation — has the show changed anything?

Taking a risk on bold strokes seems worth it when a show from a Canadian streamer goes on to make over $1.4 million from a limited theatrical release across 945 movie theaters in early November screenings. The show’s cultural relevance and staying power are a breakthrough, but a year after its premiere, it seems very little has been learned so far.

entry.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t
entry.summary: Rockstar's record-breaking 'GTA VI' has Hollywood worried about the attention economy. But comparing video games to movies sells both art forms short.
entry.content:
“Grand Theft Auto VI” took less than 24 hours to generate $3.79 billion in global sales. That’s roughly 15 percent of the year’s worldwide box office — in under a day.

But Hollywood’s biggest concern about games might not be what else consumers are spending their money on. It could be just how many days, weeks, or even months people end up playing “GTA VI” instead of streaming movies or TV on other platforms.

Even before Rockstar’s record-breaking launch on November 19, entertainment news outlets like TheWrap were asking whether the game studio’s historic release would seriously disrupt the attention economy. Several analysts echoed that concern in their own industry assessments, warning investors that the sprawling open-world adventure could monopolize living-room airspace until well after the holidays.

Related Stories
Frederick Wiseman’s Complete Filmography to Be Distributed by Janus Films
Movie Theaters in 2026: Filmmakers and Exhibitors on What’s Good, What’s Bad, and What’s Changing

There’s a sort of delicious irony in realizing a game named after a felony has Hollywood panicking about stolen screen time. Personally speaking, as a former video game critic who now mostly covers film and television, I’m fascinated by the competition for both audience engagement and consumer interest.

Still, that particular side of “GTA VI” discourse drives me up the wall. Games, movies, TV shows, and social media feeds do indeed battle for our attention, and the business of entertainment is ultimately all about influencing how strangers use their free time.

Rather, the issue lies in the assumption that one hour spent with one type of story is automatically equivalent to another hour spent with an entirely different medium — and that comparing those numbers tells us a thing about what either is really worth.

Failure to Launch (Thursday)

Last Thursday, I was at my favorite bar, catching up with a friend visiting from Seattle, when she got up to greet someone else. Scrolling on my phone, I opened a DM from my old coworker that said he was… already playing “GTA VI”? That couldn’t be!

Confused, I quickly searched “GTA 6 release date” and discovered I wasn’t just a few hours away from entering Vice City — but that I was already a full day behind the rest of the gaming world. Yes, Rockstar had spent more than a decade preparing its masterpiece, and I had somehow missed the actual drop like a tricky freeway exit.

I really should’ve known better, too. I’d preordered “GTA VI” and downloaded it on my PlayStation days earlier, but even $79.99 deep, I was caught off guard by the sudden arrival of Lucia and Jason, who, even welcome, had seriously complicated my night.

Never one to miss a groundbreaking moment in a fake place, I ran home to my apartment, determined to make up for lost time using whatever post-bar energy I had. (As it turns out, that wasn’t much.)

There’s something weirdly prudish about Hollywood’s anxiety over just how much time “GTA VI” fans might spend playing it — as though immersive and interactive narratives were an indulgence taking hours away from more legitimate entertainment. Games have been a major market and creative stage for decades, and still, the conversation around Rockstar’s new blockbuster brings to mind the sort of worried parents who would’ve been afraid of TV in the ’90s.

Those pearl-clutching concerns also miss a practical distinction. Playing a video game demands a different kind of physical and mental engagement than watching a movie or TV show. Admittedly, the first few minutes of “GTA VI” make that distinction remarkably easy to forget — opening on Lucia in prison for a sequence so beautifully lit and photographed that interacting with inmates feels at once totally real and like Rockstar showing off.

And yet, even in the “cinematic” wonder of that moment, rushing home left me in no state to steer a virtual boat. My first real “GTA VI” mission involved navigating choppy waters to pick up (and/or drop off, I honestly cannot remember) bricks of cocaine, but unfortunately, bro, I could not operate heavy machinery.

What felt like hours of circling checkpoints was probably closer to 15 minutes. Still, the technical wizardry bobbing across my screen clashed with my stomach contents, and I was desperate to stop. So, I turned off my PS5 and streamed “Knocked Up,” instead.

The Fast and the Frustrated (Friday)

I woke up to the sound of Katherine Heigl crowning and went to bed at 1 a.m., truly grateful that Judd Apatow’s 2007 comedy had freed me from the obligation to captain anything. But that night, sober as a judge and eager to get behind the wheel again, I remembered what the decade-plus of “GTA VI” hype was all about.

My first in-game police pursuit was astounding in its intricacy, with Leonida (i.e., Rockstar’s Florida) providing a jaw-dropping menagerie of local characters, each living out a personal drama or comedy of errors against a backdrop of boundless scenery.

Weaving through traffic and cutting down alleys, I realized I wanted the full “Fast and Furious” feeling early and often. You know, tightly choreographed fever dreams complete with stunt drivers, cinematographers, and someone other than me to call cut. But here, all I had was myself: a shitty chauffeur, a worse debut director, and a leading man who kept mistakenly jumping onto the roof of her car before getting in.

To be fair, “GTA VI” offers a truly impressive range of camera options when you decide to properly educate yourself on the system’s customizable controls. But as a woman who couldn’t keep her wheels on the road, let alone capture Jason’s stubble from a flattering angle, I was practically begging for a union rep — and a body double. Worse still, I was getting more and more worried about my girl, Lucia.

Rockstar had sold me on Jason as a good boyfriend, and I wanted to prioritize that interpretation in my playthrough. But the longer I waited for Lucia to get out of prison, the more convinced I became that she might never be coming back. Had I missed a mission? Decapitated the wrong innocent bystander? Whatever had gone wrong in my game, uncertainty powered Jason’s decline.

I robbed a woman after she refused my offer to help with her broken-down car. I took surprising pleasure in dispatching adversarial gang members. After a seemingly infinite number of crashes, I cared less about playing the romantic lead than about combining my growing enthusiasm for scuba diving with organized crime.

In a movie, that sort of moral deterioration might suggest a carefully constructed character arc. In “GTA VI,” it mostly reflected my own impatience. Rockstar had given me the raw materials for a compelling love story, but the longer I waited for Lucia, the more willfully criminal my version of Jason became. By Friday night, I was having a good time — but I was also getting critically hardened, and increasingly convinced I’d done something wrong to derail the romance I craved.

Out Sick in Vice City (Saturday)

Around 3 a.m. on Saturday, I was throwing up into my toilet with the word “WASTED” practically hovering above my head in enormous white letters. My plans to spend the weekend robbing old ladies and getting gradually pissier with the absent Lucia had been derailed by a profoundly gross bout of what seemed to be food poisoning.

Yeah, it was a real bummer, dog. But unable to muster the constitution for a car ride, scuba diving, or the next step in my budding drug empire, I settled for fixing up Jason’s rickety house and lifting weights on his back deck. Nauseous, I even briefly considered finishing Lucia’s bedroom, but gave up after getting stuck picking just one color from a trio of offscreen paint samples. (I didn’t know her well enough to know which one she’d like, and fighting a fever, that felt like an argument in the making.)

There was something genuinely lovely about occupying Rockstar’s beautifully realized environments without any particular objective in mind. Even under the weather, I understood why I’d seen so many people on social media comparing “GTA VI” to “slow cinema,” a style of filmmaking that finds meaning in naturalistic observation and drawn-out routines.

Its more intimate moments sometimes reminded me of Sean Baker’s “The Florida Project,” too, with its colorful vision of the Sunshine State smashing together the faded appeal of amusement parks and painful hallmarks of everyday desperation.

That’s a lot to contend with when you’re sick, though, so I turned on “The Hunting Wives” (another gloriously lurid piece of modern American satire!) and, while scrolling through social media, I was struck by a contrast.

Eight episodes of “The Hunting Wives” could simply wash over me. To get the same experience from “GTA VI,” I’d have to hunt through Vice City and its vast collection of in-universe media myself. Both had plenty to say about contemporary America. Only one required me to do much of anything to hear it.

So I was genuinely surprised when I began encountering livestreams on TikTok of people playing through later stages of the “GTA VI” story, including a scooter-stealing mission I’d just discovered but hadn’t tried yet. Then I caught a glimpse of someone playing as… Lucia?!

I scrolled away immediately. Having spent Friday convinced I’d sabotaged the romance through my own choices, I was relieved to see I was still on track, but simultaneously annoyed that someone else’s playthrough had spoiled part of my plot.

Still, I couldn’t stop laughing at the online debate over whether “GTA VI” was too woke, or whether Rockstar had successfully tricked millions of players into simulating healthy relationships. I’d bought the game partly because I wanted to participate in a massive cultural moment, and here I was, too sick to play but still in the thick of things — watching it unfold through Netflix, TikTok, and strangers whose versions of Vice City were already far ahead of mine.

It was exciting, irritating, occasionally informative, and even without my controller, I found myself making decisions about how I wanted to play later. (One person, for example, painted Lucia’s bedroom peach, a choice I disliked so much that I made both a mental and literal note to go with green in the end.)

Till Death Do We Restart (Sunday)

By Sunday night, I was finally feeling well enough to enjoy the entertainment I’d been trying to consume all weekend. Lucia had come home in my playthrough, and exploring their relationship together made “GTA VI” click in a way no amount of aimless driving could.

At a lavish yacht party, interacting with other guests became an opportunity to figure out what sort of couple these two actually were. Were Jason and Lucia the kind of boyfriend and girlfriend who did drugs together? Would romantic jealousy be an issue, or were we cool with [wink] that?

Suddenly, I wasn’t waiting for Rockstar to tell me what their connection meant. I was actively deciding, and having thoroughly mastered the mechanics of walking around without looking like a complete lunatic by then, I was putting some swag into it.

A particularly sexy jet-skiing sequence made an impression, with Jason holding onto Lucia as she drove instead of the other way around. It was a sweet little reversal of gender norms, and the kind of affectionate character detail I’d been waiting to discover. Even better, it was happening in a game that seemed to understand exactly how much I wanted to drive its love story.

Then came the Carly Rae Jepsen car chase.

Glossy and expensive, our borrowed vehicle reflected the neon lights of Vice City like a scene from “Blade Runner.” With 2015 chart-topper “Run Away with Me” blasting from the speakers, Lucia and Jason were living out the spectacular criminal romance I’d been hoping for. Skyscrapers towered around our blossoming love, and I was riding high…

… Until I smashed us into a cement divider and Jason’s head exploded.

As the game reset and made my sudden brush with vehicular homicide a thing of the past, I found myself laughing like gunfire alone in my apartment. I was suddenly orchestrating a crime of continuity no movie could ever get away with — and it was one of my favorite “GTA VI” moments yet.

Great movies and TV shows often succeed by creating characters who sincerely feel like real people. Rockstar’s new release is exceptionally good at that. But an equally extraordinary connection between art and its audience can emerge from acknowledging that the people experiencing your story have their own needs, limitations, and personalities, too.

That’s the fundamental difference between this extraordinary simulator and a fantastic film. At its best, cinema invites you to inhabit a vision so singular it could only belong to someone else. A great video game gives you the tools to make someone else’s vision singularly your own. That takes a degree of commitment that doesn’t always accommodate the realities of being a person, like, oh say, racing to the bathroom with your digestive system in active, contaminant-born revolt.

Even so, when I think about the hours I spent with “GTA VI” this weekend, I’m not particularly interested in how much other “content” I could have been watching instead. No filmmaker could have anticipated the precise emotional satisfaction I’d get from that magenta-hued highway catastrophe, and, purely from a practical standpoint, no self-respecting artist should have to.

Rockstar built Vice City over the span of a decade, but that spectacularly stupid scene in all its accidental skull-smashing glory was mine — proof there’s a world of difference between commanding someone’s attention and handing them the keys.

entry.title: Frederick Wiseman’s Complete Filmography to Be Distributed by Janus Films
entry.summary: All 45 feature films from documentary legend Frederick Wiseman have been acquired for North American distribution by Janus Films.
entry.content:
If you wanted to be a completionist for the movies of documentary legend Frederick Wiseman, or if you have a blind spot for Wiseman’s formalist portraits of American institutions dating back decades, today is your lucky day.

Janus Films has acquired the North American distribution rights to the complete collection of 45 feature films from Wiseman’s career dating back to his seminal “Titicut Follies” in 1967, and Janus plans to distribute all of them beginning January 1, 2027. Janus already has a library that includes the works of Agnès Varda, Ingmar Bergman, Akira Kurosawa, Chantal Akerman, and Edward Yang, so Wiseman finds himself in good company.

Related Stories
Movie Theaters in 2026: Filmmakers and Exhibitors on What’s Good, What’s Bad, and What’s Changing
Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival Shorts Programmer, Dies at 56

Specific distribution plans haven’t been announced yet, be it whether these films are going to be seen theatrically, via streaming, or on physical release. But Wiseman’s early films, everything from “Titicut Follies” in 1967 through “State Legislature” in 2007 have been restored in 4K by Wiseman’s Zipporah Films. “La Danse” (2009) through his final feature “Menus-Plaisirs – Les Troisgros” (2023) will be available in their original digital formats.

This is the first time any distributor other than Zipporah Films is licensing Wiseman’s work in North America, so the hope is that the late documentarian can now reach an even greater audience. It wasn’t until as recently as 2024, that Wiseman’s movies were even all available in digital formats.

“We couldn’t imagine a better home in North America for Frederick Wiseman’s films than with Janus Films,” said Karen Konicek of Zipporah Films. “It has been an honor to work alongside Fred for so many decades, producing and distributing his films. As Zipporah Films continues as the rights holder and distributor of the Wiseman Collection, we very much look forward to this new partnership with Janus Films and are excited to collaborate with them.”

“We are honored and thrilled to be the first distributor, in the US, outside of Zipporah Films, to be entrusted with licensing one of the greatest bodies of work in American cinema” said Peter Becker, President of Janus Films and Criterion. “We’re looking forward to presenting these monumental works, theatrically, to new audiences across the country.”

Wiseman passed away earlier this year in February 2026 at 96 years old. Not only was he one of the most influential documentarians in American cinema, he was one of the most prolific considering the 45 features he independently produced, directed, and edited over his 50-year career.

In 2016, Wiseman received an Honorary Oscar for lifetime achievement from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Board of Governors for his “masterful and distinctive documentaries [that] examine the familiar and reveal the unexpected.”

IndieWire spoke with Wiseman in 2025 as Lincoln Center prepared a retrospective of all his early films as part of the 4K restoration effort. He spoke about the attention to detail in his editing and his examination of each institution and its layers, despite the enormous length of many of his films.

“The subjects I choose to make films about are complicated, and I think I have an obligation when I’ve been given permission to make a movie about a place to have the final film reflect the complexity of the institution and not just be some superficial, banal representation of the institution,” he said.

The full list of titles acquired by Janus for North American distribution is below:

“Titicut Follies” (1967), “High School” (1968,) “Law and Order” (1969), “Hospital” (1970), “Basic Training” (1971), “Essene” (1972), “Juvenile Court” (1973), “Primate” (1974), “Welfare” (1975), “Meat” (1976), “Canal Zone” (1977), “Sinai Field Mission” (1978), “Manoeuvre” (1979), “Model” (1980), “The Store” (1983), “Deaf” (1986), “Blind” (1986), “Racetrack” (1985), “Adjustment & Work” (1986), “Multi-handicapped” (1986), “Missile” (1987), “Near Death” (1989), “Central Park” (1990), “Aspen” (1991), “Zoo” (1993), “High School II” (1994), “Ballet” (1995), “La Comédie-Française ou L’amour joué” (1996), “Public Housing” (1997), “Belfast, Maine” (1999), “Domestic Violence” (2001), “Domestic Violence 2” (2002), “The Last Letter” (2002), “State Legislature” (2007), “La Danse: The Paris Opera Ballet” (2009), “Boxing Gym” (2010), “Crazy Horse” (2011), “At Berkeley” (2013), “National Gallery” (2014), “In Jackson Heights” (2015), “Ex Libris: The New York Public Library” (2017), “Monrovia, Indiana” (2018), “City Hall” (2020), “A Couple” (2022), and “Menus-Plaisirs, les Troisgros” (2023).

entry.title: Movie Theaters in 2026: Filmmakers and Exhibitors on What’s Good, What’s Bad, and What’s Changing
entry.summary: IndieWire speaks with filmmakers running their own theaters, like Kevin Smith, and hears plans for reopening for the Cinerama Dome.
entry.content:
In 1948, movie studios held a monopoly in entertainment, owning the means of producing and distributing films, and the theaters themselves. The 1948 Paramount Decrees (named after the studio that pioneered the vertical integration) required studios to give up one of the three options. They decided to give up exhibition. The choice was easy: With low margins on ticket sales and the need to constantly bring audiences in, who wanted to run a movie theater?

70 years later, movie studios again faced the possibility of giving up on exhibition. The rise of streaming was said to bring about the end of theaters as we know them. But the COVID-19 pandemic brought exhibition to its closest brink of extinction yet.

Related Stories
Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival Shorts Programmer, Dies at 56
Will Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting Help Land Him His First Oscar Nomination?

“COVID allowed people to acknowledge their inner recluse,” Tim League, the co-founder and former CEO of Alamo Drafthouse, told IndieWire.

After the global pandemic, lockdown protocols forced movie theaters to close for months. The luxury theater chain Arclight shuttered all its locations within weeks. Locations closed at a variety of companies, including Alamo Drafthouse. Some theaters survived off of private rentals. Even as theaters slowly reopened, COVID protocols required leaving some seats empty, meaning not all tickets could be sold.

“I think there was no right move,” League added. “We laid most of our people off. We spent a lot of energy trying to build up a TVOD streaming platform which didn’t entirely work for a lot of reasons… And so we went through bankruptcy, and it was rough. We just ran out of money.”

“There really was no strategy,” said Greg Laemmle, owner of the California-based independent theater chain Laemmle Theatres. Since Los Angeles did not allow private rentals, the company stayed afloat via concessions, pop-up events, and some virtual cinema opportunities. “It was all just trying to understand how we can maintain contact.”

Exhibition became such an unappetizing business that many of those who jumped on board the irony-fueled GameStop stock inflation of 2021 also bought shares of AMC Theatres, bringing the company to an all-time high in valuation.

But years later, the theater market is experiencing a rebirth. Driven by new theater operators and new kinds of theatrical experiences, the contemporary exhibition landscape looks very different from 10 years ago.

Theater operators paint a picture of an industry that is no longer weathering a storm. Instead, they reveal the trends driving theaters to thrive and the issues with the model that won’t seem to die.

Artists Turned Exhibitors, from Quentin Tarantino to Kristen Stewart

The first high-profile artist-led theater acquisition was Quentin Tarantino’s purchase of the New Beverly Cinema in Los Angeles. The director had previously helped fund his childhood theater to keep it afloat before buying the cinema outright and taking over as programmer in 2014. The purchase of the 300-seat New Beverly was partly fueled by Tarantino’s desire to preserve what the digital era sought to make extinct: celluloid projection. Since the director’s acquisition, the theater proudly boasts that it screens only on film, usually 35mm.

Tarantino declined to comment on this story.

A few years later, COVID-19 brought a new threat to movie theaters. A similar mission-driven attitude took hold in a new crop of directors and artists: to protect not just how movies are screened, but to ensure audiences can still see them in communal spaces.

Independent film director Kevin Smith bought his hometown theater in Atlantic Highlands, New Jersey, in 2024. The Atlantic Twin Cinema was a five-screen multiplex Smith grew up going to, housed in a building over 100 years old. But over time, nearby multiplexes threatened to drive the theater out of business. When Smith’s friend Ernie O’Donnell told him the theater would be torn down to build condos, he resolved to help save it.

“Anything I ever learned about myself I never learned in a classroom, and I certainly didn’t learn it sitting in a church,” Smith told IndieWire. “But mostly everything I know about myself I learned sitting in the darkness of that theater, looking up at the great white mirror and seeing life reflected back at me.”

Smith invested $450,000 and partnered with several friends to buy the theater, rebranding it as Smodcastle Cinemas. While he mostly lives in Los Angeles, Smith travels to Jersey every month to work on the theater.

Smith described how the finances of owning a theater in a small town may not always reflect larger box office trends. “Avatar: The Way of Water” opened in 2024 and eventually grossed over $2 billion, making it one of the most successful films in history. But at Smodcastle Cinemas, they only sold 12 tickets opening weekend.

At Smodcastle, the theater has leaned into what Smith calls “The business of Kevin Smith.” This includes Q&As of his films featuring Smith and his collaborators like Justin Long for a “Tusk” screening, and Tracy Morgan for the 15th anniversary of “Cop Out.” The theater started a film festival to help showcase local New Jersey cinema. Smith was working on selling a reality show about the theater’s day-to-day operations, similar to the seven-season run of “Comic Book Men” filmed inside the comic shop he owns, but said progress has stalled.

“I love calling up Ernie and being like, ‘How many seats [have we sold] so far?’ And he’ll be like ‘120 out of 230,’ and I’m like, ‘All right man, I gotta put 90 more asses in seats. Let me see if I can jump on a radio show… go over to Manhattan and jump on “Good Day New York” and try to get the word out,’” Smith explained. “It’s fun, but it is definitely fucking work. I have a feeling Quentin don’t work nearly as fucking hard at his theater.”

Smith elaborated on the work it takes to keep the theater running, “We all got together and saved the theater, man. But it was the worst financial fucking decision I ever made,” Smith said. “Owning a movie theater in the 21st-century post-COVID [world], it’s a dicey proposition at best… We became a nonprofit theater because the movie theater’s never going into fucking profit.”

The nonprofit model has become an increasingly popular option for keeping theaters alive. In 2012, Los Angeles video rental store Vidiots transitioned to a nonprofit to stay afloat, recasting its mission around film preservation, protection, and education. The organization later received heavy support from Megan Ellison’s Annapurna Pictures, which kept the company running for two years after it shuttered its store in 2017.

“If you go across the country, you’re seeing a real boom in nonprofit or community-supported movie theaters,” said Laemmle. He highlighted the Tasveer Film Center in Seattle, which reopened the former Ark Lodge Cinemas in 2025 due to support from a local nonprofit that had run a South Asian film festival.

“Why not form a community organization that augments ticket sales with other sources of revenue, or that can take advantage of their not-for-profit status and do the enhanced kind of programming that you can’t do at a for-profit business?” said Laemmle.

The high costs of running a movie theater are also evident in one of the latest major theater purchases by an artist. Director Jason Reitman led a group of 30 filmmakers — including Christopher Nolan, Guillermo del Toro, Steven Spielberg, and Chloé Zhao — to purchase the historic Village Theater in Westwood, Los Angeles, in 2024. Since rebranding as Directors Village, the theater has partnered with the film nonprofit American Cinematheque, which will handle its programming.

The $12 million acquisition in 2024 rescued the historic theater after its lease with its former owner expired. The filmmakers will pour an additional $25 million into renovating the theater, which was open for programming in summer 2026 but closed in October and will reopen in 2027. The project required an alleged six-figure minimum buy-in from the artists involved.

Jason Reitman declined to comment through a representative, citing that it is too early to discuss plans for the theater’s renovation. American Cinematheque did not respond to requests for comment.

Jason Reitman and Co. also looked into purchasing the adjacent Bruin Theater but were ultimately deterred by the extensive cost of renovations, as previously reported by IndieWire.

The list of artists owning theaters is only growing. Kristen Stewart purchased the historic Highland Theatre in Los Angeles in February 2026 and plans to restore the space into a hub for the L.A. film community. Tarantino bought a second LA theater, the Vista, in 2021. Martin Scorsese, Ethan Hawke, and Frances McDormand joined the advisory board of the Upper West Side Cinema Center to turn the former Metro Theater on Broadway in New York City into a five-screen arthouse theater, funded by New York City grants and donors like the Kate Capshaw and Steven Spielberg Hearthland Foundation.

The trend highlights a new form of altruism by creatives seeking to keep theaters alive. But even if the business isn’t financially valuable, there is an argument for artists to be seen as patrons of their craft. “As more and more movie theaters start closing down, every filmmaker is from somewhere, and every filmmaker has their hometown theater,” said Smith. “And if you have a degree of success where you’ve got some side hustle loot and whatnot, what a great way to spend your money.”

Studios Get Back in the Exhibition Game

In 2019, the Department of Justice marked the Paramount Decrees for termination, citing changes in the studio system structure and film market that rendered the law obsolete. In August 2020, while most theaters in the United States were shuttered, the Department of Justice ended the decree.

In November 2019, Netflix announced it would lease New York City’s historic Paris Theater, three months after a notice of closure was posted. In May 2020, the streamer bought the closed Egyptian Theatre in Hollywood to be co-programmed between the studio and its previous operator, American Cinematheque. In October 2021, Netflix also announced it would take over the lease of the Bay Theater in the Pacific Palisades.

These acquisitions had a touch of irony considering Netflix made a name for itself by rejecting theatrical exhibition. The streamer did not abide by the then-standard 90-day exhibition window before making its films available on the service. The Academy Awards require week-long theatrical runs to make films eligible for awards. Major chains like AMC Theatres and Regal Cinemas refused to show Netflix films (and still do on occasion; Regal and Cinemark recently announced they will not screen “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” due to the shortened theatrical window). But just as it became legal for Netflix to enter the theater market, it did. By becoming an exhibitor, it no longer needed major theaters to show its films.

“Netflix needs screens in the L.A. and New York market,” said James Huntsman, the co-founder of distribution company Blue Fox Entertainment Group, which purchased two former iPic theaters in June 2026. “I don’t care if you are Netflix, it’s really hard to get a screen in both of those two markets… So if you’re Netflix and you have six movies that are coming out between October and December and they all need qualifying runs of seven days, full runs in both markets, now you start seeing why they’re interested in screens.”

Amazon Studios opened The Culver Theater — the former Culver City Arclight location, which shuttered in March 2020 after the company went bankrupt due to closures from the COVID-19 pandemic — in December 2022. The theater screens a mix of new releases, repertory screenings, and hosts premieres for Amazon MGM Studios’ television shows and movies.

In October 2026, Paramount Pictures announced it took over the lease for the Bay Theater, which has been closed since the 2025 Palisades fires. The new theater, opened in November 2026 and operated by The Lot, similarly offers first-run theatrical releases from all studios, along with dine-in food.

“We’ll see if it really develops into anything more than just a novelty for them,” said Laemmle about studios purchasing individual theaters. “[They’re] one-offs and just being able to want to say that they’ve got something. But I don’t sense there’s going to be a more prolonged investment, but if it happens, it’d be great.”

The most high-profile studio entrance into the movie theater market was Sony Pictures Entertainment’s acquisition of theater chain Alamo Drafthouse in 2024. Founded by Karrie and Tim League in 1997, the company made its name as an offbeat theater option with dine-in service and strict rules against talking and phone use in its theaters.

“I think we came to it from people who loved movies but didn’t really love our options with chain theaters that we had around,” said Tim League. “We were always looking at how we can build this and build a community around sharing movies we love.”

Alamo Drafthouse began talks with Sony Pictures Entertainment in late 2023 before completing the sale in 2024.

“It was kind of essential to find a new partner as soon as we ran out of money,” said League, who has since stepped back from daily operations at the company and remains involved as Strategic Advisor.

“Why it was appealing for us as a company with our board prior to deciding that Sony was the right acquirer for us is partly because of what that also meant in terms of resources that Sony could offer… Not only in terms of Sony [being] a very big, well-capitalized company but reputationally, very financially stable, [and] very well respected in the space,” said Michael Kustermann, CEO of Alamo Drafthouse and head of Sony Pictures Experiences.

Sony is not involved with day-to-day operations of Alamo Drafthouse. But the parent company’s ownership is evident in occasional special programming, such as airing the Season 4 finale of “Breaking Bad,” which Sony’s TV division produced, in Alamo theaters in September 2026 to celebrate protagonist Walter White’s birthday.

But the largest initiative made possible by Sony’s ownership was the July 2026 announcement that Alamo Drafthouse would purchase the historic Cinerama Dome theater in Hollywood and the attached 14-screen multiplex.

“This has been the white whale for Alamo for a long time,” said Kustermann. He explained Alamo was interested in the location before the Sony deal but didn’t have the financial means to acquire a new flagship location. But after a couple of years of interest and conversations that did not progress, Alamo reached back out after the Sony deal and began serious talks in 2025.

The company plans to operate the Cinerama Dome screen unlike traditional Alamo theaters. Dine-in service will not be offered. Kustermann said that the renovations will be minimal, aiming to keep a similar seat count. The iconic curved screen that defined Cinerama projection will remain, and reprints of films screened in Cinerama such as “It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World” will be part of the programming slate.

Renovations to the multiplex will include adding one or two 70mm projectors, karaoke rooms, an updated bar, and an aesthetic redesign inspired by the theater’s 1960s decor.

Blue Fox Entertainment was founded in 2015. The North American distribution and film sales company distributes over a dozen films a year across a variety of genres.“Exhibition is where all the glamour is, right?” said Huntsman. “Distribution is very labor-intensive; you’re supplying content to a theater, to a platform, to DVD. It’s very back office, administrative.”

“I only got into distribution as a way to get into exhibition,” Huntsman explained, adding that Blue Fox Entertainment bought its two theaters to combine the company’s passion for film and enter a new market. “I make no qualms. I’m in the money business, but I’m using movie theaters and film distribution and film sales to do that.”

When the dine-in theater chain iPic went bankrupt in 2026, Blue Fox bid on six of the 12 available locations and ultimately purchased the Westwood, Los Angeles, and New York City theaters. The dine-in service was removed, but each location has a full-service restaurant attached that does not require a cinema ticket.

By rebranding as The Cinemas, Huntsman aims to turn the theaters into viable assets that can make money beyond box office revenue. “I have private events, I have two restaurants at these locations, I do advertisements around the exterior. So if you put all that together, it’s not a bad business. If it was just a standalone straight movie theater, it’s a tough market.”

The Troubles with the Theater Business

The economics of why so many new independent theaters are popping up can be traced to a basic reality of the business, according to Laemmle: the simplicity in bringing a theater back to life. “You don’t need to pay anything to acquire inventory. It’s not like opening a bodega where you’ve got to fill it with stuff. You get a film, you promise to pay a percentage of the box office to the studio, and suddenly you’re in business.”

Ticket split rates can vary per title. The rate can be anywhere from 30% for repertory screenings to over 60% for a blockbuster Disney release. Some studios send a range of split rates that can be negotiated; others (like Disney) set a non-negotiable rate.

A film’s success can also affect how much a theater owner makes per ticket sale. Speaking to this summer’s releases, Huntsman said that the underperformance of films like “Supergirl” and “Moana” meant he received a larger portion of the box office. But for big hits like “Toy Story 5,” theaters get a smaller piece of the action.

Studios can also control exhibition through clean policies: the practice that if a theater licenses a certain film, it must be on screen when the theater is open. These policies can be especially detrimental to single-screen theaters in rural areas, effectively limiting the variety of films a community can show.

At Smodcastle, Smith planned special programming with Vulgathon, a marathon of all the films in his View Askew universe from “Clerks” to “Clerks III” in order. But while ticket sales were tracking to sell out all 900 seats across five screens, Disney said that if the theater did not leave a screen open for the second weekend of “Deadpool and Wolverine,” the studio would not send them the film to screen for its opening weekend.

“So we had to leave one screen open, for fucking ‘Deadpool’ and shit, that did not sell out,” Smith said.

Advertising revenue also dropped dramatically post-COVID, according to Laemmle. He estimates that the company currently makes 25% of its pre-pandemic revenue through theater advertising. “Ad agencies had a budget that they allocated for in-theater advertising in the pre-pandemic world. All of a sudden, movie theaters were closed so they just took those same ad dollars and moved them somewhere else…That was a significant source of contribution to the bottom line that’s really gone.”

Loss of advertising revenue forces theaters to find new revenue streams. For some major chains like AMC and Regal, that includes pay-for-play trailer programming: where studios can pay to put trailers for their upcoming releases in front of new titles. This also incentivizes longer trailer blocks that can run up to 30 minutes.

Other major sources of revenue for theaters are concessions, which can offer high margins for cheap snacks like popcorn and pre-packaged candy. Beer and wine sales have also been a major boost of revenue for Laemmle Theatres.

The other option: Lean into alternative programming that may not incur as high ticket splits. The Cinemas has been experimenting with testing various repertory titles across different genres to figure out what titles will draw people back into theaters. Their upcoming lineup for November and December 2026 includes “Boyz in the Hood,” “When Harry Met Sally,” and “The Lord of the Rings” trilogy.

For Huntsman, the need for theaters to diversify revenue reflects the current model for how studios release films. “When I grew up seeing movies in theaters primarily in the ‘80s, there were like three studio releases every week…There was always the rom-com, the horror film, the action film, the indie film…Now it’s ‘Fast and the Furious’ comes out, and nobody releases anything for three weeks.” Huntsman added, “So in terms of profitability, [that’s] part of why we’re making the theater a destination.”

Elevated Experiences

Rising labor, rent, and electric bills over the last few years have made it harder for theaters to improve their margins. In a search for more profits, theater operators have taken on new initiatives to upgrade the technologies and amenities associated with theater-going to bring in crowds looking for a more premium experience, with varying degrees of success.

For Alamo Drafthouse, the Sony-owned company received complaints from longtime fans in 2026 after introducing mobile ordering to its theaters, replacing the original pen-and-paper method that involved more engagement with servers. Instead, guests scan QR codes to place orders that are sent directly to the kitchen.

This move drew ire from the Alamo community, who saw it as hypocritical to the company’s prominent No Phones policy. The company’s subreddit became flooded with users saying they wouldn’t be returning to the theater amid the changes. Actor Elijah Wood, an Austin local who frequently appeared at events put on by the chain, criticized the new system, calling it “truly awful” in a post on X.

The company described the QR code ordering system as part of a larger plan to ensure long-term stability and keep innovating the experience, citing past changes like introducing reserved seating and ending its adults-only policy.

An Alamo spokesperson said that the company has not laid off any staff due to introducing QR codes and that it allows servers to handle more tabs. They added the core of the decision was to protect wages and jobs for the company’s staff working 12 months a year, but that QR codes will allow them to hire fewer seasonal staffers.

Tim League declined to comment on the QR code system.

While Alamo Drafthouse pioneered the dine-in model for theaters, League’s newest business venture is to bring exhibition into the luxury space. He launched Metro Private Cinema in 2025, a 20-screen theater in New York City’s Chelsea neighborhood that specializes in small, private theater experiences with fine-dining menus to accompany the films.

Theaters range from four to 20 seats. Bookings start at four hours, and food packages are added to the price. Guests can choose between new releases, special holiday-themed programming, or a specific movie, plus a la carte food.

“Since the dawn of cinema, it has been being tightly packed into a large room with a bunch of strangers,” said League. “So what if we kind of flip that around, and it’s you’re surrounded by friends. And how does that change the experience?”

Pricing for the experience can vary. Example packages on the website list costs starting around $200 per person. When asked about introducing a luxury price point into the theater market, League explains that costs align with the high prices commonplace in the city. “Our meals are $115 for a 13-course meal, which is very much in line with New York pricing.” League added, “We have built a more higher-end, expensive model, but I think what we’re offering is not ridiculous.”

If companies are not expanding the price-point of concessions, the other option is to expand the theatrical viewing experience itself. Sony Pictures Entertainment launched Cosm, a 364-seat immersive theater with an 87-foot curved screen, in 2024. Tickets are roughly $50, with some including themed food options. And massive Las Vegas entertainment complex The Sphere received over $400 million in revenue from sales of its multisensory AI-edited run of “The Wizard of Oz.”

In recent years, audiences have shown growing interest in premium theater presentations. Major studio blockbusters are expected to have exclusive IMAX runs. Films like “Sinners” and “The Odyssey” have driven a rise in interest in IMAX 70mm screenings, letting audiences see movies in the format directors intended.

CJ 4DPlex, the developer of premium screening formats ScreenX and 4DX theaters, reported a 26% increase in revenue in the first half of 2026 compared to 2025. Their technology includes 270-degree panoramic presentations or immersive 4DX theaters with moving seats and water effects. Ticket surcharges can range from $3 to $7 for ScreenX showings and up to $10 for 4DX tickets, compared to a traditional 2D ticket.

But the desire to jump into premium formats is not universal. Laemmle said his theaters have no plans to offer advanced presentations. “We’re not necessarily engaged in the large format with the higher ticket price because we believe that movie-going should be something that’s done regularly…Moviegoing historically was the cheapest form of out-of-home entertainment, and we believe it should stay that way.”

Can Cinemas Stay Alive?

The movie theater industry has always existed on a wire’s edge. Owners and monopolies have come and gone. Projection trends like Cinerama and Vistavision had their moments before becoming obsolete. Television, VHS, DVDs, and streaming have all carried the threat of being the final innovation that would put theatergoing in the past forever.

“The death of our industry has been predicted since the ‘50s with every new turn,” said League. “I just think there’s [now] pressure not to lose sight of the fragility of being an awesome third space.”

2026 is currently on track to have the best box office performance globally since 2019, with the year expected to end with $35.7 billion in global ticket sales.

For Huntsman, the increase is corollary to the output the studios offer: that the box office success of “The Odyssey” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is more tied to quality than any other metric. “Anyone that says, ‘Oh, movie theaters are back,” they didn’t go anywhere. There just weren’t any good movies playing.”

At Laemmle Theatres, the biggest draws of the year have been indie success stories, with films like “You Can See Everything,” “NAZA,” and “Filipiñana” bringing the theater some of its largest ticket sales.

Speaking with a variety of theater operators, the common thread in running a successful theater wasn’t what was on the screen. The key was understanding each theater’s audience. For Laemmle Theatres, it’s typically older people who go to the movies often and have a wide variety of tastes. At Metro Cinema, it’s New Yorkers with the funds to splurge on an elevated experience for special occasions. And at Smodcastle, it’s Kevin Smith fans looking for programming only Kevin Smith can provide.

The full scale of how COVID-19 changed culture has yet to be fully realized. But the renewed investment in owning and innovating movie theaters speaks to a broader desire to safeguard community spaces where people can exist between work and home. The theater industry’s revenue streams are more diversified than they’ve been in years. The allure of owning a movie theater isn’t just about making money; public goodwill has added intangible rewards for exhibitors for keeping theaters alive.

Or as Smith said, “It’s good for the heart, good for the soul, good for the optics, good for the brand.”

entry.title: Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival Shorts Programmer, Dies at 56
entry.summary: Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival shorts programmer and filmmaker, had died after a brief illness. He was 56.
entry.content:
Mike Plante, a filmmaker and 25-year veteran of the Sundance Institute, died Tuesday after a brief illness. He was 56.

At Sundance, Plante worked as a Shorts Programmer and was a familiar, warm-hearted presence at festival screenings and events.

“Mike was a treasure to the Institute, the Festival, and our independent film community,” Sundance Festival Director Eugene Hernandez and Director of Programming Kim Yutani said in a joint statement. “His sense of wonder and humor were matched by boundless enthusiasm and curatorial excellence. Our Festival’s Short Film Program and the Sundance Film Festival Short Film Tour were shaped by Mike’s energy and superb taste in movies. Mike’s roots at Sundance Institute, and his relationships within our organization and festival, run deep. He will be remembered and deeply missed as a true cinephile, a filmmaker, a champion of short films, movie theaters, and film culture.”

Related Stories
Will Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting Help Land Him His First Oscar Nomination?
Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’

In addition to his work at the festival, Plante directed the 2011 feature documentary “Be Like an Ant,” which followed a Vietnam War veteran who builds a house around a mobile home to handle winter living. He also directed numerous shorts including “The Polaroid Job” (2016), which looked at his parents’ work running a paid event-photography studio in the 1980s. It is available to watch on the New York Times’ Op-Doc website.

Amy Redford, the daughter of Sundance founder Robert Redford and a board member of the festival, called Plante, “a visionary.” “Through his extraordinary curatorial talent, he launched countless storytellers through the vital medium of short film, many of whom have gone on to become some of the world’s most enduring artists,” she said. “Mike embodied the Sundance ethos and played a critical role in preserving the continuity of its values. He was unfailingly generous with his time and mentorship, and a talented creator in his own right. But Mike’s most enduring legacy is his kindness. It was, and remains, the first thing people say about him. His passing is a profound loss not only to the Sundance community, but to all those fortunate enough to have known and loved him. He will be deeply missed.”

Along with directing, Plante produced feature documentaries by other directors, including “Scrap Vessel” (2009) and “Giuseppe Makes A Movie” (2014). Plante started working for film festivals as a programmer in 1993, eventually joining Sundance in 2001.

In 1998, he started the film zine Cinemad, which he wrote for and produced a podcast. The site championed indie and under-seen movies. Plante also wrote “Sensation Cinema: The Audacious, Defiant History of Louis Sher and the Art Theatre Guild,” which looked at an influential arthouse theater owner and distributor. It was a world that Plante knew intimately. In 2024, he was named head of distribution at The Beverly Theater, an independent cinema in Las Vegas, Nevada. He also worked with the CineVegas Film Festival with Trevor Groth, another Sundance vet, as its Director of Programming.

Plante is survived by his mother, Barb.

entry.title: Will Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting Help Land Him His First Oscar Nomination?
entry.summary: Will Rob Pattinson's Bond Casting Land Him his First Oscar Nomination?
entry.content:
How will Robert Pattinson‘s casting as James Bond affect his Oscar chances? The hard-working star, who was established by the “Twilight” franchise, has ricocheted from Christopher Nolan projects (“Tenet” and “The Odyssey”) and the DC franchise’s “The Batman” (“Part Two” is shooting in London) to riskier indies like the Safdies’ “Good Time” and Robert Eggers’ “The Lighthouse.”

This award season, Pattinson was juggling three long-shot potential Oscar nods: Best Actor for A24’s marital deconstruction “The Drama,” and Supporting Actor for two Snidely Whiplash villains, lead suitor Antinous in Universal’s blockbuster “The Odyssey” and shape-shifter Scytale in Warner Bros.’ “Dune: Part Three,” respectively. His best chance at an Oscar nomination, though, was always for his creepy lead turn as TV journalist Chris Hansen in “Primetime,” another A24 release.

Related Stories
Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’
‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

When Daniel Craig was cast as James Bond during the awards tour for Steven Spielberg’s “Munich” (2005), the immediate result was a marked increase in attendance at all screenings, recalls one veteran publicist. “There was a different before-and-after energy,” he said. That did not land Craig a nomination, however. The only Bond to score an Oscar nod and win after a long and storied career was Sean Connery (“The Untouchables”). Playing Bond does not lend an actor cred with the Academy. But it does extend a career.

The impact for Pattinson, who is ubiquitous in online media, is the same. At this point, most awards voters will have seen “The Odyssey,” but those seeing the Christopher Nolan blockbuster for the first time will view the actor differently. “He will have heightened scrutiny,” said one studio Oscar expert. “Clearly he is being tapped to anchor a franchise. For the actors [branch], he will be someone to reckon with.”

Clearly, fewer people have screened “Primetime.” Pattinson’s Bond ascension will push the movie up in the must-see rankings. “Bond probably gets more people to watch the movie,” said one Oscar strategist. “That’s half the battle. The goal is to get people to watch the movie. But the movie has to do the work.”

At the box office, “Primetime” has fared better domestically ($47 million) than abroad ($12 million), which is significant given an Oscar voting pool of more than 10,000 voters, one-quarter of whom are international. How will “Primetime” do with the upcoming critic votes? Or BAFTAs, which will reveal the international tale? And SAG’s Actor Awards, where, at this stage, Gold Derby has “Digger” star Tom Cruise edging out Pattinson? The race between those two actors is “squishy,” said Debra Birnbaum, Gold Derby editor-in-chief, who distinguishes between early season “hopedictions” and “real predictions.”

It helps to remember that the Academy is just starting to catch up with the contenders. The experts on Gold Derby (I’m one), at this stage, have seen way more movies than the site’s users or the Academy. Later in the season, Gold Derby users and experts are more in sync. That’s why we should take with a grain of salt the recent ascension among the Gold Derby users to number five for Best Actor contender Pattinson. They’re responding to publicity. The experts have him at seven. The same is true for the betting site Kalshi’s odds. Their accuracy improves the closer you get to the Oscars. At this stage, their bettors haven’t seen everything. And the key Oscar season markers, from critics’ groups to Guild awards, haven’t played out.

The American Cinematheque came out way ahead by honoring Pattinson with its annual award fete, set to take place on February 9, 2027. Tables are selling out and Bond studio Amazon/MGM — and Hollywood — will be there in force.

While Pattinson has never been an actors’ actor, he’s a hugely bankable global movie star. He’s going to keep us interested for a long time.

entry.title: Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’
entry.summary: Guitarricadelafuente talks 'La Bola Negra,' Los Javis' breakup, writing the song 'La Nieve,' and more.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: The following interview contains spoilers for “La Bola Negra.”]

With a head of hair, lithe frame, and the soft eyes Caravaggio would’ve loved if the Italian painter were Spanish, pop star Guitarricadelafuente is having a monumental year on- and off-screen. The gay 29-year-old songwriter finished touring his sensational, sensually charged second album “Spanish Leather” earlier this fall, and only just a few short months after his screen debut, “La Bola Negra,” won a Cannes top prize, got scooped up by Netflix, and entered the awards season fray.

Oscar talk is in the wind, not just for his performance as queer closeted trumpeter Sebastián, who joins the Nationalist forces during the Spanish Civil War to survive, but for writing the original song “La Nieve.” The sweeping ballad ties together the film’s three story threads that convene around queer Spanish playwright Federico García Lorca’s incomplete text: 1932, 1937 (Sebastián’s storyline), and 2017. Born Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, he’s now a meme thanks to his stage and screen sobriquet, which means “little guitar of the fountain.”

Related Stories
‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier
John Turturro, Carrie Coon, Guitarricadelafuente, and Peter Gamble to Receive SFFILM Honors

Guitarricadelafuente’s performance balances both hushed repression and eventually unleashed emotions throughout “La Bola Negra,” as Sebastián nurses wounded (and handsome) Republican soldier Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau, a more established actor in Spain). They fall for each other in the process, in a furtive romance mostly framed in stolen glances and tacit looks — in other words, the sort of good old-fashioned gay yearning that’s made movies like “Brokeback Mountain,” “Call Me by Your Name,” and “God’s Own Country” so popular. “La Bola Negra” is, by now, one of the highest-grossing Spanish movies ever to play in Spain, and it’s a major Oscar contender in select theaters as it gears up for its early December Netflix streaming premiere.

IndieWire spoke to Guitarricadelafuente over Zoom where, behind him, an oversized window frame flanked the waves gently rushing up to Miami Beach. Below, we discuss his songwriting process for “La Nieve,” witnessing the breakup of directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo (which happened during filming), and how he overcame his fears to make his auspicious screen debut. That’s all while balancing a proudly out music career where his sexuality is front and center. Plus, watch an exclusive video about his role in the film at the bottom of this story.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You’ve been all over the world with “La Bola Negra,” from Cannes in May to Toronto and, now, Miami Beach for this virtual junket interview. You’re used to being all over the place. You also toured your album this year. Did that help you prepare for promoting the film?

Guitarricadelafuente: I would say that kind of, in a way, because there’s something that I see as very similar to going and talking about the movie and talking about your character, which is something very similar to when you’re going around touring with your album. I think it’s more difficult because you need to talk about yourself and not just about playing a character because the music you make comes from a very profound place, and you need to talk about many things that go inside of you.

This is your acting debut, and there’s Oscar chatter for both your performance and the song you wrote for the film, “La Nieve.” Do you watch the Academy Awards in Spain?

Not that much recently, but I remember when I was studying architecture in college, I used to stay up late at night doing projects. I remember staying up until 3:00 a.m. and with my friends, we were doing our little houses, and we would put the television on, and see the awards. But that was one of the only times that I stayed up late, or that I used to stay up late to see the awards, because you always receive that in Spain in the morning after.

You signed up for the movie without a script. What was the pitch that the Javis gave you? You knew you’d have to learn the trumpet.

They didn’t tell me that I had to learn an instrument because it was going to be originally something that I already knew how to play, but they wanted to make it more difficult. So they said, “OK, why don’t you try a trumpet?” But yeah, the first pitch, there was not much about it. They told me about “La piedra oscura” by Alberto Conejero, which was the original play where the characters of Rafael and Sebastián appear.

I just knew that it was going to be set against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, with Lorca being so present. … They didn’t convince me, but I was so moved by how they were so confident that I could do it because I was so frightened and I wasn’t sure at all, but it was their vision. I admired them so much from before. I knew that they’ve worked with many nonprofessional actors, and people acting for the first time. So it was something that I just threw myself into.

You were frightened about whether or not you could deliver as an actor, or was it the material?

I was spending all of my time making music and touring, and it was very time-consuming and exhausting. … I didn’t know if I could put myself into that experience because I thought the proper way to dig into that role was to put your soul into it.

They were looking for someone who was openly gay for this role, right? There’s a spectrum of sexualities among the cast. Miguel Bernardeau, your scene partner, is straight.

Well, I don’t even know if we talked about that at any point because it was just assumed that I was. [Laughs] I don’t know if that was a condition. I think it was something that, to be more faithful to the story, had to happen. At the time that they approached me with the role, I was finishing my last album, “Spanish Leather.” It represented an imaginary — but not that imaginary — journey of a young gay man who comes out from his village and puts himself out to the world, discovering who he is and where he belongs.

Many people would know my music, but I would realize that not many people knew that I was gay even. There’s a big, not sexual, but I would say sensual component to [“Spanish Letter”] and this process of growing up and sexual [awakening]. So it was very special in a way to play this role … it’s something that you don’t get that much, maybe in Spain, just to see things where you can get referenced with or reflected with.

Los Javis broke up during production. Did they communicate that to the cast? How did you find out?

It was so weird because I don’t know if I’m stupid or what, I didn’t even notice. I would hear obviously so many rumors, but … you couldn’t tell that they were apart because they were acting as one. And I couldn’t believe that they were breaking up with the intensity of that shoot. It was like, “How on earth are they going to split up in the middle of this craziness and this madness?”

But I don’t even remember when they told us. I think it was at the end of the shoot. We would eventually know that something was going on. I couldn’t believe it. How have you managed to carry this shoot? But that also represented how moving this story was to them.

People were gossiping at that point.

Of course. Even when they reached out to me with the role, I would hear rumors, and I was like, “How is this going to be possible if they’re so tight together?” It was inevitable because they are so well known in Spain, that rumors would arrive.

Miguel has probably 10 years of acting experience that you don’t have. Was he helpful as a mentor, as well as an onscreen romance?

The first time that we met, it was actually when he was doing his audition because the only character that was clear in the movie was Sebastián. We had to test how this approach was going to be with the real Rafael, because this very tight and intimate connection had to happen. He didn’t know that I was going to play Sebastián, and he just appeared in the rehearsal room. And I thought there was a very special instant connection there, that I think we’re obviously very different, or we come from very different backgrounds or different ways of seeing the world.

But there was a beauty in that because obviously I saw him as this wonderful, beautiful, talented, and professional actor that I could anchor myself in. He’s all the time lying on a bed [on screen]. And so he has to say so many things without being able to move. We were both left a lot of freedom on set and to try and to make errors. The room would get empty, and it was just Los Javis, Miguel, and I.

Were you writing the movie’s theme song, “La Nieve,” during production?

It was a very long process from the beginning, when I was told to write the song. I don’t think of me doing a song as in I get into a room and say, “OK, what I’m going to talk about right now?” And then I get a lyric, and I go back home. This Film has so many stories in it, and to try to be faithful to all of them and try to unify them in a thread, in a song, was very difficult. I was listening at the time, before they reached out to me, to Spanish Civil War songs.

It was actually a queer singer of the time who was called Rolando Alarcón. There were songs played with parlor guitars that were [made] to be sung on the waterfront. We started preparing the role with Los Javis. Lorca had to be very present also in this because he’s all over the place. He’s pretty omnipresent all of the time, surveilling what’s going on. And you had to pay a homage to him because, in the end, “La bola negra” was this unfinished script that he was writing.

I had to live my character in my own skin and properly carry that emotional baggage that he was holding. And it wasn’t until the end of the shoot, when we were in Cantabria living for two months … I obviously had this melody in my head, but when this scene with the firing squad happens, and [SPOILER ALERT] Rafael dies, it was a combination of all of that emotional journey that the character was living.

I would arrive home that day and start playing a melody on a piano and mumbling some lyrics, and I would send this to Los Javis, and I didn’t know that they were going to use this to unify the three stories that go on in the movie. And it was a way for me to let all of that emotion go.

This song will now have to be part of every setlist you perform. It’s your “My Heart Will Go On.”

I hope it turns into that. I wish to be 50 years old and be in Madrid and be singing that. That would be so beautiful. Because I feel that I was just playing in Madrid my last concert one month ago, it was kind of the closing chapter of this “Spanish Leather” tour, and the film was just released one week before that. And so I got the chance to play “La Nieve” there for the first time. After that, it was very emotional because you would hear 18,000 people singing to that. It was like goosebumps. After that, people would be commenting on TikTok, “So Sebastián had the chance to finally be a musician and get to Madrid and perform.” That’s kind of like a closing of the thread, a very beautiful thing.

“La Bola Negra” is also one of the highest-grossing Spanish movies to play in Spain ever. Have you been able to go home and experience that?

We were in Spain those first two weeks until we had the last concert in Madrid, and then we went to Toronto and all over the place. And that was a very special week because I was at my sister’s wedding. You could feel something in the air. There was a communal excitement, and people of all ages, all different ages, going to the cinema, or even people, like aunts of mine, who haven’t been to the cinema in 10 years, to see how that’s happening is something that makes us very proud.

For me, the Spanish premiere was more important because that’s all Spanish people’s lives. Everybody has been linked to that moment of time, it’s like their ancestors. So the Spanish were going to be the most critical of it. But to see how young people, old people, people from different backgrounds go and you suddenly have this sense of communion was something spectacular that you could see in the streets. Like older ladies and young queer guys coming up to you, it’s just incredible.

What are you doing next? Do you want to keep acting?

Yeah. It’s been a crazy time. I’m having the time to even make new music and to, I don’t know, to see what I’m able to, because even three years ago… I would oblige myself to be quiet and rest to be able to feel inspired. But now it’s all these hectic times that are making me feel so inspired, and to share that time and put it into making art.

You’re thriving on the chaos.

I’m thriving on the chaos.

“La Bola Negra” is now in select theaters will start streaming on Netflix on Wednesday, December 2.

entry.title: John Turturro, Carrie Coon, Guitarricadelafuente, and Peter Gamble to Receive SFFILM Honors
entry.summary: John Turturro, Carrie Coon, Guitarricadelafuente, and Peter Gamble will receive 2026 SFFILM Awards Night prizes.
entry.content:
Awards season will be making a stop in San Francisco on December 7 for the annual SFFILM Awards Night, honoring four artists who’ve made an impact this year.

John Turturro, acclaimed this year for his performance in “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” will receive the Maria Manetti Shrem Award for Acting, named for the Italian-American philanthropist. (Turturro will also receive IndieWire Honors recognition on December 3.) Carrie Coon, who made a big-screen splash this year in “The Liberation,” will receive the Katie & Todd Traina Award for Acting. The SFFILM Award for Virtuosity will go to “La Bola Negra” breakout star and beloved Spanish pop singer Guitarricadelafuente. Finally, the Nion McEvoy & Leslie Berriman Award for Storytelling goes to “I Play Rocky” screenwriter Peter Gamble.

Related Stories
Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work
The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’

Presenters include “La Bola Negra” directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, and “I Play Rocky” star Anthony Ippolito (all of whom are also being feted by IndieWire Honors in December).

SFFILM Awards Night will take place on Monday, December 7, 2026, at San Francisco’s Gateway Pavilion at Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture.

Anne Lai, SFFILM’s executive director, said, “Film has a rare power to change how we see the world. SFFILM exists to celebrate it and to build its future. At Awards Night we do both. We honor artists whose bold, generous storytelling defined this year in cinema, and we raise the resources that power our work all year long, from students in Bay Area classrooms to the filmmakers we fund and mentor. I’m thrilled to welcome our honorees to San Francisco, where the future is always being created, and film is the gateway.”

“Carrie, Guitarricadelafuente, Peter, and John each bring a distinct sensibility and an uncommon command of their craft to the screen this season,” said Jessie Fairbanks, SFFILM’s director of programming. “We selected this group because they represent the range of talent and creative perspectives that make cinema so compelling, and their work speaks to the thoughtful, nuanced, and often unexpected films that make a season memorable. They bring a fearlessness, determination, and depth of perspective that we are proud to celebrate at SFFILM.”

Last year, Benicio Del Toro, Kristen Stewart, Wunmi Mosaku, and Scott Cooper all received SFFILM prizes. The event serves as a fundraising opportunity for the Bay Area nonprofit film organization that also hosts the San Francisco International Film Festival.

entry.title: Want to Attend a Major Film Festival with IndieWire? Applications for Our 2027 Intensives Are Now Open
entry.summary: Apply today for IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Student programs in Cannes, Venice, Austin, and London.
entry.content:
Anyone who attends film festivals regularly will tell you that it’s never too early to start thinking about your travel schedule. If you’re a student, recent grad, or emerging professional interested in joining IndieWire at Cannes, Venice, SXSW, or SXSW London in 2027 through our Future of Filmmaking Intensives, it’s a great time to apply and secure your spot for next year. The earlybird deadline for all four programs is next Monday, November 30. And be sure to use the code IWBLACKFRIDAY26 to waive your app fee.

Apply to all of our 2027 film festival Intensives here.

Not sure which program is right for you? Keep reading for more info about each one.

Related Stories
Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work
The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’

SXSW Intensive

Dates: March 14-21, 2027

There’s no way to describe SXSW until you’ve attended it. The annual Austin, Texas event is a celebration of every creative discipline. You have a conference featuring some of the leading executives and creatives from every major industry on the planet, a music festival with a history of discovering major indie talent, a comedy festival that programs nightly live performances, and a major presence from the gaming and VR industries — and that’s before you even get to the first-class Film and TV Festival that hosts major world premieres. It’s an unforgettable experience that belongs on every entertainment professional’s bucket list, but navigating it on your own can be overwhelming. But attending through IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking SXSW Intensive can help you cut through the chaos and get the most out of the experience. We’ll help you curate a program of film screenings, panels, and networking events in order to get the full SXSW experience while still feeling like you advanced your career in a focused way. More info here.

Cannes Intensive

Dates: May 9–23, 2027 (14 day intensive) or May 16-23, 20217 (seven day intensive)

The program that started it all.
