The American Pavilion has been a fixture of the Cannes Film Festival for over 35 years, providing educational programming, networking opportunities, and hospitality right on the Croisette. Our Future of Filmmaking Intensive, presented in partnership with The American Pavilion, gives you the best possible view of the action at the world’s biggest film festival. In addition to attending film screenings at the festival, attendees will have access to all of IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking programming at the Pavilion. Panels frequently include filmmakers and actors with major movies playing at the festival, as well as executives and decision makers who can share insights about the direction the industry is heading in. Plus you’ll have access to AmPav’s signature parties and events, including our annual Queer Night and our Emerging Filmmaker Showcase. More info here.

SXSW London

Dates: May 23-30, 2027

The SXSW brand is no longer limited to Texas! If you prefer your multidisciplinary festivals with a European flair, you can attend SXSW London 2027 with IndieWire. The London event features the same multicultural approach to film, tech, music, and more while highlighting a different slate of films and TV shows from around the world. The program also gives you a chance to experience one of the world’s great cities during a week when decision makers from around the world descend upon it. More info here.

Venice Intensive

Dates: September 2027

Cannes might be the world’s largest film festival, but the honor of being the world’s oldest festival belongs to Venice. Taking place in one of Italy’s most storied cities, the festival serves as an unofficial kickoff to the fall movie season and the Oscar race, as critics and distributors get their first real looks at what will become some of the biggest films of the year. Our Venice Intensive places you right in the center of the excitement while giving you ample time to experience the history and culture that Italy has to offer. In addition to festival accreditation, the program features cultural excursions including trips to the island of Murano and Burano. It provides the best of Hollywood and the best of Europe in one unforgettable experience. More info here.

entry.title: Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work
entry.content:
The making of “Project Hail Mary” was a miracle on par with the outer space rescue mission that Ryan Gosling is tasked with pulling off. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s bestselling novel manages to be epic without ever losing its intimacy, as Gosling traverses the galaxy and saves the world with only a very lovable rock acting alongside him. The final product was a complicated blend of practical effects, on-set puppetry, and a healthy dose of VFX magic.

Incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved. The puppetry team lead by James Ortiz had to fit into very small spaces, which frequently meant they showed up in the frames. Visual Effects Production Supervisor Mag Sarnowska and her team were tasked with removing all of the puppeteers. But as she explained during the VFX panel at IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables, it was a small price to pay for the way it enhanced Gosling’s acting performance.

Related Stories
The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’
‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner

“It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said. “It was great to have them there, but it did not work out sometimes. Our sets were really, really tiny. Having five people there to puppet Rocky was hard sometimes. But to everyone’s point, having something there in the frame was so helpful, especially for Ryan to act to. The eyeline? That’s a real thing. Even though our Rocky didn’t have eyes, a person’s brain makes it easier to figure out where the eyes would be just by having that constant relation between Rocky and Ryan.”

Sarnowska — who will share the Innovation Award at the IndieWire Honors with Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, and Paul Lambert — explained that having a real reference point for VFX sequences is what ultimately makes the most effects-heavy sequences feel real.

“In Ryan’s space, he has to be in the xenonite glass, so having reflections, adding the glass, it was a lot of work,” she said. “But having that real thing, having that reference, even if we had to replace it, that was so important. Because we knew what Rocky would look like.”

More coverage from our Craft Roundtables can be found here.

entry.title: The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’
entry.summary: Composer Bostic and director Rita Coburn discuss the varied influences on the music of their documentary, from spirituals to classical references.
entry.content:
Rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial. In her storytelling, Coburn shares with her subject a talent for distilling complex ideas and expressing them with force and clarity; the result is a movie that fully honors the breadth and depth of Du Bois’ achievements as a groundbreaking Black writer, historian, and activist.

One of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works.

Related Stories
‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner
26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’

The scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives. “Rita and I talked about what types of touchstones we needed to define the narrative musically,” Bostic told IndieWire. “There was the regional touchstone, the era-specific touchstone, the interior emotional aspects that we wanted to heighten with music. Then there’s always the discovery process as you begin to create.”

For Bostic, that discovery process is one of the most exciting aspects of film composing. While she had a number of reference points as she began work on the score, she soon found herself following intuition to take them in different directions than initially intended. “There’s always what I call the hands-on-the-clay moment,” Bostic said. “You have your list, and you have your frame of reference, but the process is fluid.”

According to Coburn, Bostic’s ability to bring a historical perspective to her scores made her an ideal collaborator for the film. “Kathryn pulled from the region of Great Barrington [where Du Bois was born] as well as New York in that time period, and then what was happening with the African-American community that Du Bois was entering,” Coburn said. “There wasn’t gospel then, so you were looking at a small group of Black people going to the churches there in New England. What were they listening to, and therefore what was he listening to?”

Bostic drew on the music of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a Black a capella ensemble that inspired Du Bois, but then moved in a completely different direction to explore his time in Berlin, when he encountered and fell in love with classical music. She also incorporated Wolof music from Senegal and the Gambia in collaboration with Coburn’s daughter, who studied classical music and worked in the music department on “Rebel with a Cause.”

“She found a Senegalese professor online who worked with her so she could sing the Wolof,” Coburn said. “Kathryn and I agreed that we had to put the Wolof in the film because it connects Du Bois to his Ghanaian roots. But we had to find it, and we wanted it to be as authentic as possible.”

For Bostic, the challenge was taking an audience from 2026 and presenting the music in a way that would recreate the way in which Du Bois experienced it over a hundred years earlier. “There’s the historic arc of the times, as well as what he’s experiencing emotionally,” Bostic said. In the places where her score was informed by spirituals and the work of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the composer tried to tie the emotional subtext to the context in which she knew Du Bois was consuming the music.

“When he went to Fisk University, his mother had recently died,” Bostic said. “So that music was a wellspring for his grieving, and I think that depth of sorrow and the catharsis that resulted from that sorrow inspired the sort of deep self-reflection that became such a deep part of who he was. That self-reflection led to a basic decency and humanity, and even now I think of him as being light years ahead of people in the way he embodied justice. I want to shine a light on that.”

Coburn felt a similar sense of purpose, especially since the more she dug into Du Bois’ life the more she realized how relevant his insights were to America in 2026. “He speaks to this current time,” Coburn said, adding that the importance of Du Bois’ work gave her own work a sense of urgency and responsibility. “I knew that it might be 20 or 30 years before we get another Du Bois documentary. I hope not, but I looked at his life and knew that I had to do the best job that I could. We did everything we could for Du Bois because we felt he had done everything he could for us.”

The greatness of “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is that it brings the viewer into Du Bois’ perspective as his world view continues to expand over a 95-year life, and the music is a major part of that subjectivity.

“Kathryn understands that music is a character in any documentary, and her music embodies the character of W.E.B. Du Bois,” Coburn said. “ In the music, we had to grow with him. We had to expand with him. We had to see that his love of Rembrandt and his understanding of classical music, of music that came from an Asian culture, that all of that was important to him. We were catching up with him, and he was driving us.”

“W.E.B. DuBois: Rebel with a Cause” is currently streaming on the PBS app and website.

entry.title: ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier
entry.summary: Milton S. Hershey gets the Angel Studios treatment in a deranged and decidedly vanilla piece of "values-based entertainment."
entry.content:
A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul.

Related Stories
‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind
‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Grade: D

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.
